questions.question: What is Docker and why do we use it?
questions.answer: Docker is a containerization platform that packages applications and their dependencies into containers. We use it to solve the 'works on my machine' problem — containers run identically across development, testing, and production environments regardless of the underlying infrastructure.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
questions.answer: A Docker image is a read-only template — a blueprint containing application code, dependencies, and configuration. A container is a running instance of that image. The relationship is the same as AMI to EC2 instance: the image is the static template, the container is what's actively running.

questions.question: What are the two main components of Docker?
questions.answer: Docker CLI (Command Line Interface) — the tool users interact with to type commands like docker run, docker build, docker ps. Docker Daemon (dockerd) — the background service that actually builds and runs containers. The CLI sends instructions to the Daemon.

questions.question: What is a Dockerfile?
questions.answer: A Dockerfile is a text file containing step-by-step instructions for building a Docker image. Key instructions include FROM (base image), WORKDIR (working directory), COPY (copy files), RUN (execute commands during build), EXPOSE (document ports), and CMD (startup command).

questions.question: How do you persist data in Docker containers?
questions.answer: Using Docker Volumes or Bind Mounts. By default, container data is ephemeral — it's lost when the container is deleted. Volumes store data on the host machine outside the container lifecycle. Critical for databases: -v myvolume:/data/db ensures MongoDB data survives container deletion.

questions.question: What is Docker Hub and how does it differ from AWS ECR?
questions.answer: Docker Hub is the default public container image registry — anyone can push/pull images. AWS ECR (Elastic Container Registry) is a private registry within your AWS account, secured by IAM policies. ECR is preferred for enterprise workloads where you don't want proprietary images publicly accessible.

questions.question: What is Docker Compose and when would you use it?
questions.answer: Docker Compose manages multi-container applications via a docker-compose.yml file. Instead of running multiple docker run commands manually, one docker-compose up starts all containers with correct networking and volumes. Use it for local development and simple multi-service deployments like frontend + backend + database.

questions.question: What are the Docker network types?
questions.answer: Bridge (default) — private network on the host, containers communicate using container names. Host — container shares the host machine's network directly. Overlay — spans multiple hosts, used in Swarm/Kubernetes. None — no networking, fully isolated container.

questions.question: How do you make a Docker container accessible from the internet?
questions.answer: Port mapping (-p hostPort:containerPort) maps a host port to a container port. Example: docker run -p 8080:80 nginx maps host port 8080 to container port 80. You also need to open the corresponding port in the EC2 Security Group for internet access.

questions.question: Why can't Docker alone handle production workloads?
questions.answer: Docker lacks production-critical features: no auto-scaling when traffic spikes, no self-healing when containers crash, no built-in load balancing across containers, no zero-downtime rolling deployments, and if the host EC2 goes down, all containers go down with it. Container orchestration tools like Kubernetes, ECS, or EKS fill these gaps.

questions.question: Walk me through a situation where you had to troubleshoot a Docker permission error on a Linux server.
questions.answer: (Situation) After SSH-ing into an EC2 Ubuntu instance, running docker ps returned 'permission denied'. (Task) Restore Docker functionality for the ubuntu user without using sudo for every command. (Action) Checked Docker daemon status with sudo systemctl status docker — it was running. Identified the real issue: the ubuntu user wasn't in the docker group. Ran sudo usermod -aG docker ubuntu followed by newgrp docker. (Result) Docker commands worked immediately without sudo, and the fix persisted across reconnections.

questions.question: Describe a situation where you had to containerize an application and push it to a private registry.
questions.answer: (Situation) A Python Flask web app needed to be deployed on EC2 consistently across dev and prod environments. (Task) Containerize the app and store the image privately in AWS ECR. (Action) Wrote a Dockerfile with FROM python:3.11-slim, COPY, RUN pip install, EXPOSE 5000, CMD. Built with docker build -t my-app:v1 . Authenticated to ECR using aws ecr get-login-password. Tagged and pushed the image to ECR. Attached an IAM Role to EC2 instances so they could pull images without credentials. (Result) Deployments became consistent and automated — no more environment-specific bugs.

questions.question: How did you handle data persistence for a database container that was being frequently updated?
questions.answer: (Situation) A MongoDB container was running for a development project, but data was lost every time the container was recreated. (Task) Implement persistent storage without changing the application code. (Action) Added a named Docker volume to the docker run command: -v mongo-data:/data/db. In Docker Compose, added volumes configuration at the service and top-level. Tested by inserting data, deleting the container, recreating it, and verifying data persisted. (Result) Data survived all container lifecycle events. Documented the volume backup procedure for production environments.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you managed a multi-container application deployment.
questions.answer: (Situation) An e-commerce project had three services: React frontend, Node.js backend, and MongoDB database, each needing to be containerized and networked together. (Task) Create a development environment where all three services start with one command. (Action) Wrote Dockerfiles for frontend and backend. Created docker-compose.yml defining three services with depends_on ordering, a shared custom bridge network for inter-service communication, a named volume for MongoDB, and port mappings for external access. (Result) docker-compose up started the entire stack. Developers had a consistent environment with one command, eliminating setup time and environment inconsistencies.

questions.question: Describe how you would migrate from Docker containers on a single EC2 to a managed orchestration service.
questions.answer: (Situation) A single EC2 running 8 Docker containers directly became a single point of failure — when the EC2 went down, everything went down. (Task) Migrate to a managed orchestration service to achieve high availability. (Action) Evaluated ECS vs EKS — chose ECS since the team was AWS-native and didn't need Kubernetes portability. Pushed all images to ECR. Created ECS Task Definitions from existing docker run configurations. Created ECS Services with desired count 2 for high availability. Configured Application Load Balancer in front of ECS Services. Enabled Fargate launch type to eliminate EC2 management. (Result) Application became highly available across multiple AZs with automatic failover, auto-scaling, and zero manual container management.

questions.question: Walk through a production incident where a container kept crashing and how you resolved it.
questions.answer: (Situation) A payment service container kept crashing in ECS, causing failed transactions. (Task) Identify root cause and restore service within SLA. (Action) Checked ECS Service events — saw containers failing health checks. Used docker logs (via CloudWatch) to view container output — found OOM (Out of Memory) errors. Checked Task Definition — memory was set to 256MB but the service needed 512MB for peak load. Updated Task Definition with 512MB memory. Deployed new task definition. Verified containers stayed healthy through monitoring. (Result) Service stabilized immediately. Added CloudWatch alarm on container memory to proactively catch similar issues.

questions.question: What is Kubernetes and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform that automatically manages containers in production. It solves the production limitations of Docker alone: provides auto-scaling (scale containers based on traffic), self-healing (auto-restart crashed containers), load balancing (distribute traffic across replicas), and zero-downtime rolling deployments. It's cloud-agnostic — works on AWS, Azure, GCP, or on-premises.

questions.question: Explain the Kubernetes cluster architecture.
questions.answer: A Kubernetes cluster has two layers. Control Plane (the brain): API Server (single entry point for all requests), etcd (key-value store holding all cluster state), Scheduler (decides which Node runs each Pod), Controller Manager (maintains desired state). Worker Nodes (execution layer): Kubelet (agent bridging Control Plane and container runtime), kube-proxy (manages network rules), Container Runtime (containerd/CRI-O), Pods (where containers actually run).

questions.question: What is the difference between ECS and EKS?
questions.answer: ECS (Elastic Container Service) is AWS's proprietary container orchestration — simpler, no Kubernetes knowledge needed, tight AWS integration, best for AWS-only workloads. EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) is AWS-managed Kubernetes — AWS manages the Control Plane, you use standard kubectl/YAML, skills and manifests are portable to other clouds (Azure/GCP). Choose ECS for simplicity within AWS; choose EKS when you need Kubernetes or cloud portability.

questions.question: What is AWS Fargate and when should you use it?
questions.answer: Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers — no EC2 instances to provision or manage. AWS handles all server infrastructure; you just provide the container image and CPU/memory requirements. Use Fargate when: you want zero server management, workloads are variable (pay-per-task), you're a startup prioritizing speed over cost optimization, or you need quick deployment without infrastructure setup.

questions.question: How does Kubernetes self-healing work technically?
questions.answer: The Controller Manager continuously runs control loops that compare actual cluster state against the desired state declared in your Deployment. If actual replicas (e.g., 2) < desired replicas (e.g., 3), the Deployment Controller creates a new Pod spec, the Scheduler assigns it to a Node, Kubelet on that Node instructs the container runtime to start the container. This happens automatically within seconds of a failure, with no human intervention.

questions.question: Explain RBAC in Kubernetes.
questions.answer: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is Kubernetes's authorization mechanism. It controls who can do what in the cluster. Key components: Role/ClusterRole defines a set of permissions (verbs like get, list, create on resources like pods, services). RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding binds a Role to a user, group, or ServiceAccount. ServiceAccounts are identities for Pods. Best practice: grant least privilege — give each component only the permissions it needs, nothing more.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Deployment and a StatefulSet in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: A Deployment manages stateless Pods — Pods are interchangeable, have random names, and can be rescheduled to any Node. Suitable for web servers, APIs. A StatefulSet manages stateful applications where Pod identity matters — Pods have stable network identities (pod-0, pod-1), stable storage, and ordered deployment. Used for databases (MongoDB, Cassandra) where each instance has a unique role or data.

questions.question: How does container image promotion work in a CI/CD pipeline with Docker and AWS services?
questions.answer: A complete pipeline: Developer pushes to feature branch → Pull Request triggers Jenkins/GitHub Actions → CI pipeline runs unit tests → docker build creates the image tagged with git commit SHA → docker push sends image to ECR → CD pipeline (CodePipeline or ArgoCD) detects new image → updates ECS Task Definition or Kubernetes Deployment with new image tag → rolling update replaces containers one by one with zero downtime → health checks validate new version → old containers are terminated. Failed health checks trigger automatic rollback.

questions.question: A microservices application has 10 services. How would you architect the container strategy on AWS?
questions.answer: I would use a layered approach: Images stored in ECR (one repo per service, tagged by git SHA and environment). Orchestration with EKS for Kubernetes portability, or ECS if team is AWS-focused. Fargate for variable-traffic services, EC2 node groups for compute-intensive, steady workloads. Namespaces to separate dev/staging/prod. HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) on each service based on CPU/custom metrics. Service mesh (AWS App Mesh) for inter-service communication with observability. CloudWatch Container Insights for centralized logging and metrics. ALB Ingress for external traffic routing. This provides scalability, cost efficiency, and operational visibility.
